issues.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser of immovable property in another person’s actual possession is deemed to have notice of that person’s title, including an earlier contract, when the purchaser fails to inquire into the nature of the possession.
material_facts: The claimant was in actual possession of the property as a tenant and alleged that the owner had earlier agreed to sell it to him.

The subsequent purchasers knew that the claimant was in possession but relied on the owner’s account of the claimant’s relationship to him and the location of documents, and made no inquiry into the nature of the claimant’s possession.
The courts below found that the purchasers had no actual knowledge of the earlier agreement; the Supreme Court held they would be deemed to have notice of it if it was found to be true and valid.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers would be deemed to have notice of the earlier agreement if that agreement was found to be true and valid; lack of actual knowledge did not resolve the question of notice.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a subsequent transferee is outside the class against whom specific performance may be enforced only if the transferee purchased for value, paid in good faith, and had no notice of the earlier contract. Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act defines notice to include notice arising from wilful abstention from inquiry or gross negligence, and Explanation II deems a person acquiring an interest in immovable property to have notice of the title of a person in actual possession. The principle that a purchaser must inquire into the terms on which a tenant is in possession was stated in Daniels v. Davison and followed in Faki Ibrahim v. Faki Gulam Mohidin, Mahadeo v. S.B. Kesarkar, Tiloke Chand v. J.B. Bettie & Co., Parthasaradhi Iyer v. Subbaraya Gramani, and Mummidi Reddi Papannagari Yella Reddy v. Salla Subbi Reddy.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and subsequent_purchaser_acquired_immovable_property and another_person_was_in_actual_possession and purchaser_did_not_inquire_into_nature_of_possession and earlier_contract_was_valid

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an earlier contract to transfer property.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser_acquired_immovable_: A purchaser acquired an interest in immovable property after the alleged earlier contract.
predicates.another_person_was_in_actual_possession: A person other than the transferor was in actual possession of the property when it was acquired.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_inquire_into_nature_of: The purchaser did not inquire into the terms or rights underlying the other person’s possession.
predicates.earlier_contract_was_valid: The alleged earlier contract was found to be true and valid.
predicates.purchaser_is_deemed_to_have_notice_of_ea: The purchaser is treated as having notice of the valid earlier contract.

issues.definition: When a subsequent purchaser acquires property while another person is in actual possession and does not inquire into the nature of that possession, the purchaser is treated as having notice of a valid earlier contract.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court deciding a specific-performance claim must make its own finding on the validity of a disputed contract rather than merely assume the trial court’s finding.
material_facts: The trial court found that the alleged earlier agreement existed.
The purchasers denied that the agreement was genuine and alleged that it was forged.
The appellate judge assumed the trial court’s finding was correct and decided the dispute about the purchasers’ notice without independently assessing the evidence on the agreement’s validity.
The Supreme Court remanded the matter for a fresh decision on the issue of the agreement’s genuineness and validity.
issues.conclusion: The appellate judge was required to consider the evidence and record an independent, positive finding on whether the disputed agreement was true and valid; the issue had to be decided afresh.
issues.legal_principle: Where the existence or validity of the contract grounding a specific-performance claim is disputed, an appellate court cannot resolve the claim by merely assuming the trial court’s finding to be correct; it must consider the evidence and record its own finding on that issue.

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim for specific performance.
predicates.contract_validity_is_disputed: A party contests whether the contract supporting the specific-performance claim is genuine or valid.
predicates.appellate_court_only_assumed_trial_findi: The appellate court relies on an assumed trial-court finding without independently assessing the evidence on contract validity.
predicates.appellate_court_must_make_its_own_findin: The appellate court must assess the evidence and decide contract validity for itself.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance appeal, when contract validity is disputed and the appellate court has only assumed the trial court’s finding, the appellate court must decide validity for itself.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for discretionary specific performance must be reconsidered under the governing equitable standard after the validity of the underlying contract is determined.
material_facts: The courts below had declined specific performance, relying on circumstances that included the parties’ close relationship, the difference between the alleged contract price and the later sale price, and the claimant’s conduct.
The Supreme Court remanded the case for a fresh finding on the genuineness and validity of the alleged agreement.

The Supreme Court expressed no opinion on whether specific performance should be granted and directed that the discretionary-relief question be decided afresh under Section 20(2) of the Specific Relief Act after the finding on contract validity.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court left the entitlement to specific performance undecided and remanded that question for fresh determination under Section 20(2), following a finding on the validity of the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: The court’s exercise of discretion to grant specific performance is governed by Section 20(2) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The discretionary-relief question must be considered afresh after deciding whether the contract relied on is true and valid.

predicates.specific_performance_claim_is_remanded: A claim for specific performance has been sent back for a fresh decision.
predicates.contract_validity_requires_fresh_finding: The validity of the contract supporting the claim remains to be determined.
predicates.discretionary_entitlement_to_specific_pe: The court must reconsider whether to grant specific performance after deciding contract validity.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance claim is remanded and contract validity remains unresolved, the court must decide contract validity first and then reconsider discretionary entitlement.
